questions.subject: Principles of Accounts
questions.text: Accounting is best defined as the process of
options: transporting goods from producers to retailers
recording, classifying, summarising, and interpreting financial transactions
advertising a business's products to consumers
manufacturing goods for sale to customers
questions.explanation: Accounting systematically records financial transactions, organises them into categories, summarises them into reports, and interprets the results for decision-making.

questions.subject: Principles of Accounts
questions.text: Bookkeeping differs from accounting mainly in that bookkeeping is concerned with
options: the routine recording of day-to-day financial transactions only
the preparation of a company's tax returns exclusively
the auditing of a company's accounts
the interpretation and analysis of financial statements
questions.explanation: Bookkeeping is a subset of accounting focused purely on systematically recording transactions, while accounting extends further to classifying, summarising, and interpreting that data.

questions.subject: Principles of Accounts
questions.text: Which of the following is a primary user of accounting information within a business?
options: The general public with no interest in the business
Foreign governments unrelated to the business
Management, for planning and decision-making
Competitors seeking to shut the business down
questions.explanation: Management relies heavily on accurate accounting information to plan operations, control costs, and make informed business decisions.

questions.subject: Principles of Accounts
questions.text: Which of the following is an external user of a company's accounting information?
options: The company's own accounting department
The company's internal audit staff only
Shareholders and creditors
The board of directors exclusively
questions.explanation: Shareholders and creditors are external stakeholders who rely on published financial statements to assess the company's performance, profitability, and creditworthiness.

questions.subject: Principles of Accounts
questions.text: Which professional body regulates the accounting profession in Nigeria?
options: The Nigerian Union of Teachers (NUT)
The Nigerian Medical Association (NMA)
The Institute of Chartered Accountants of Nigeria (ICAN)
The Nigerian Bar Association (NBA)
questions.explanation: ICAN is the principal professional body responsible for regulating and setting standards for the accounting profession in Nigeria.

questions.subject: Principles of Accounts
questions.text: The main objective of financial accounting is to
options: eliminate the need for any form of taxation
manufacture goods more efficiently
maximise the personal wealth of the accountant
provide accurate financial information to both internal and external users of the business
questions.explanation: Financial accounting exists primarily to communicate a business's financial position and performance clearly and accurately to those who need it for decision-making.

questions.subject: Principles of Accounts
questions.text: The going concern concept assumes that a business will
options: continue its operations for the foreseeable future, without any intention of liquidation
be liquidated within the current accounting period
cease operations at the end of every accounting year
only operate for a single transaction
questions.explanation: The going concern concept underlies most accounting practices, assuming a business will continue operating long enough to realise its assets and settle its obligations in the normal course of business.

questions.subject: Principles of Accounts
questions.text: The accrual concept states that revenues and expenses should be recognised
options: only when cash is physically received or paid
only if approved by the company's shareholders
at the end of the business's entire life
when they are earned or incurred, regardless of when cash is actually received or paid
questions.explanation: Under the accrual concept, transactions are recorded in the period in which they occur economically, not necessarily when the associated cash changes hands.

questions.subject: Principles of Accounts
questions.text: The consistency concept in accounting requires that
options: different accounting methods should be used for similar transactions
financial statements are never comparable between years
a business changes its accounting method every year to reflect new trends
the same accounting methods should be applied from one period to the next, unless a change is justified
questions.explanation: Consistency ensures that financial statements remain comparable over time by requiring a business to stick to the same accounting policies from period to period, barring good reason to change.

questions.subject: Principles of Accounts
questions.text: The prudence (conservatism) concept requires accountants to
options: recognise expenses and liabilities as soon as possible, but revenues only when they are reasonably certain
ignore any potential future losses
always report the highest possible profit figure
recognise revenue before it is earned
questions.explanation: Prudence guards against overstating a business's financial position by requiring caution: anticipate losses and liabilities early, but only recognise gains and revenue once they are reasonably assured.

questions.subject: Principles of Accounts
questions.text: The materiality concept in accounting suggests that
options: financial statements should exclude all numerical data
materiality applies only to non-profit organisations
every single transaction, no matter how small, must be reported in full and exhaustive detail
only information significant enough to influence the decisions of users needs to be disclosed in detail
questions.explanation: Materiality allows accountants to focus detailed reporting on items significant enough to affect user decisions, while very minor items can be treated more simply without distorting the overall picture.

questions.subject: Principles of Accounts
questions.text: The dual aspect (double entry) principle states that every transaction affects
options: the cash account exclusively
at least two accounts, with a debit entry and a corresponding credit entry of equal value
only a single account in the ledger
the owner's personal account only
questions.explanation: The dual aspect principle underpins double-entry bookkeeping: every transaction has two equal and opposite effects, recorded as a debit in one account and a credit in another.

questions.subject: Principles of Accounts
questions.text: The business entity concept states that a business is treated as
options: a separate accounting entity, distinct from its owner(s)
part of the government for accounting purposes
irrelevant when preparing financial statements
identical to and inseparable from its owner
questions.explanation: This concept requires that the financial affairs of the business be recorded separately from the personal financial affairs of its owner(s), even for a sole proprietorship.

questions.subject: Principles of Accounts
questions.text: The historical cost concept requires that assets be initially recorded in the accounts at
options: their estimated future market value
their original purchase cost, rather than their current market value
zero value regardless of purchase price
the price the owner wishes to declare
questions.explanation: Under the historical cost concept, assets are recorded at the actual amount paid to acquire them at the time of purchase, providing an objective and verifiable basis for accounting records.

questions.subject: Principles of Accounts
questions.text: The basic accounting equation is expressed as
options: Liabilities = Assets + Capital
Assets = Liabilities + Capital
Capital = Assets + Liabilities
Assets = Liabilities - Capital
questions.explanation: The fundamental accounting equation shows that everything a business owns (assets) is financed either by what it owes to others (liabilities) or by the owner's investment (capital).

questions.subject: Principles of Accounts
questions.text: A business has assets of N500,000 and liabilities of N200,000. What is its capital?
questions.explanation: Using Assets = Liabilities + Capital: Capital = Assets - Liabilities = 500,000 - 200,000 = N300,000.

questions.subject: Principles of Accounts
questions.text: An increase in an asset account is normally recorded as a
options: credit
neither debit nor credit
both debit and credit simultaneously in the same account
debit
questions.explanation: Under double-entry bookkeeping rules, asset accounts increase with a debit entry and decrease with a credit entry.

questions.subject: Principles of Accounts
questions.text: An increase in a liability account is normally recorded as a
options: credit
an adjustment to the capital account only
neither debit nor credit
debit
questions.explanation: Liability accounts increase with a credit entry and decrease with a debit entry, the opposite of the rule for asset accounts.

questions.subject: Principles of Accounts
questions.text: An increase in the owner's capital is normally recorded as a
options: credit
an adjustment to the asset account only
debit
neither debit nor credit
questions.explanation: Capital, representing the owner's claim on the business, increases with a credit entry, following the same rule as liabilities since capital is effectively owed back to the owner.

questions.subject: Principles of Accounts
questions.text: A ledger account is best described as a
options: single book containing only cash transactions
summary record of all transactions relating to a particular item, such as cash or a specific debtor
list of a business's employees and their salaries
document used exclusively for tax purposes
questions.explanation: Each ledger account consolidates all the debit and credit entries relating to one specific item (an asset, liability, expense, revenue, or capital), allowing its balance to be easily determined.

questions.subject: Principles of Accounts
questions.text: In double-entry bookkeeping, for every debit entry made, there must be a
options: corresponding credit entry of equal value in another account
corresponding debit entry of equal value in the same account
reduction in the total value of assets
corresponding entry only if the transaction involves cash
questions.explanation: Double-entry bookkeeping requires that every transaction be recorded twice: once as a debit and once as an equal credit, ensuring the accounting equation always remains in balance.

questions.subject: Principles of Accounts
questions.text: When a business purchases equipment for cash, the correct double entry is to
options: debit both the equipment and cash accounts
debit the equipment account and credit the cash account
credit both the equipment and cash accounts
credit the equipment account and debit the cash account
questions.explanation: The equipment account (an asset) increases, so it is debited; the cash account (also an asset) decreases as payment is made, so it is credited.

questions.subject: Principles of Accounts
questions.text: When a business receives cash from a debtor, the correct double entry is to
options: credit both the cash and debtor's accounts
debit the cash account and credit the debtor's account
credit the cash account and debit the debtor's account
debit both the cash and debtor's accounts
questions.explanation: Cash increases, so the cash account is debited; the debtor's account balance decreases as the amount owed is settled, so it is credited.

questions.subject: Principles of Accounts
questions.text: A trial balance is prepared primarily to
options: calculate the exact profit made by a business
check the arithmetical accuracy of the ledger accounts by confirming total debits equal total credits
replace the need for a balance sheet
record the first entry of a new transaction
questions.explanation: A trial balance lists all ledger balances to verify that total debit balances equal total credit balances, serving as a basic arithmetic check before preparing final accounts.

questions.subject: Principles of Accounts
questions.text: Books of prime (original) entry are used to
options: record only cash transactions exclusively
replace the need for ledger accounts entirely
record transactions for the first time before they are later posted to the ledger
summarise final financial statements at year end
questions.explanation: Books of prime entry (journals) are where transactions are first recorded chronologically, from source documents, before being subsequently posted (transferred) to the relevant ledger accounts.

questions.subject: Principles of Accounts
questions.text: The Sales Journal (Sales Day Book) is used to record
options: purchases of goods on credit
credit sales of goods to customers
returns of goods by customers
cash sales of goods to customers
questions.explanation: The Sales Journal specifically records credit sales transactions (invoices issued to customers), while cash sales are recorded directly in the cash book.

questions.subject: Principles of Accounts
questions.text: The Purchases Journal (Purchases Day Book) is used to record
options: returns of goods to suppliers
credit purchases of goods from suppliers
cash purchases of goods
credit sales of goods to customers
questions.explanation: The Purchases Journal records goods bought on credit from suppliers, based on supplier invoices received, distinct from cash purchases recorded in the cash book.

questions.subject: Principles of Accounts
questions.text: The Returns Inwards Journal (Sales Returns Book) is used to record
options: goods returned by the business to its suppliers
cash paid to suppliers
cash received from customers
goods returned by customers to the business
questions.explanation: Returns Inwards records goods that customers send back to the business, typically due to defects or dissatisfaction, reducing the amount owed by that customer.

questions.subject: Principles of Accounts
questions.text: The Returns Outwards Journal (Purchases Returns Book) is used to record
options: credit sales made to customers
goods returned by the business to its suppliers
cash sales made by the business
goods returned by customers to the business
questions.explanation: Returns Outwards records goods the business sends back to its suppliers, typically due to defects, reducing the amount the business owes that supplier.

questions.subject: Principles of Accounts
questions.text: The General Journal is typically used to record transactions that
options: do not fit into any of the other specialised books of prime entry, such as opening entries or correction of errors
are recorded exclusively in the cash book
involve only credit sales of goods
involve only cash receipts
questions.explanation: The General Journal serves as a catch-all book for unusual or non-routine transactions not covered by the specialised day books, such as opening balances, error corrections, and the purchase of fixed assets on credit.

questions.subject: Principles of Accounts
questions.text: A single-column cash book is used to record
options: credit transactions only
cash, bank, and discount transactions together
cash transactions only
both cash and bank transactions in separate columns
questions.explanation: A single-column cash book has just one money column and records only cash receipts and payments, unlike double- or three-column cash books that also track bank and/or discount transactions.

questions.subject: Principles of Accounts
questions.text: A three-column cash book includes separate columns for
options: assets, liabilities, and capital
debtors, creditors, and stock
sales, purchases, and returns
cash, bank, and discount (allowed/received)
questions.explanation: A three-column cash book tracks cash transactions, bank transactions, and discount allowed/received all in one combined book, offering a more comprehensive record than a single-column cash book.

questions.subject: Principles of Accounts
questions.text: The petty cash book is used to record
options: bank loan transactions only
small, routine cash expenses such as postage and stationery
credit sales transactions
large capital expenditures like the purchase of buildings
questions.explanation: The petty cash book handles minor day-to-day cash expenses, often managed under the imprest system, keeping the main cash book free of numerous small transaction entries.

questions.subject: Principles of Accounts
questions.text: Under the imprest system of petty cash, the petty cashier is reimbursed at the end of a period with an amount equal to the
options: amount spent, minus a fixed administrative fee
entire remaining balance in the petty cash box
double the amount spent during the period
total amount spent during that period, restoring the float to its original fixed amount
questions.explanation: The imprest system reimburses exactly what was spent, always bringing the petty cash float back up to its predetermined fixed amount at the start of the next period.

questions.subject: Principles of Accounts
questions.text: Source documents, such as invoices and receipts, are important in accounting because they
options: replace the need for any ledger accounts
are only relevant for tax authorities, not for bookkeeping
are used exclusively in the preparation of the trial balance
provide the original evidence from which entries in the books of prime entry are made
questions.explanation: Source documents (invoices, receipts, cheque stubs, etc.) provide the factual basis and evidence for recording transactions accurately in the books of prime entry.

questions.subject: Principles of Accounts
questions.text: A trial balance that fails to balance (total debits do not equal total credits) indicates that
options: the business has definitely made a profit for the period
at least one arithmetical error exists in the ledger accounts
all transactions have been recorded correctly
the business has definitely made a loss for the period
questions.explanation: An imbalance in the trial balance signals that an error affecting only one side of an entry (a one-sided error) has occurred somewhere in the ledger, requiring investigation.

questions.subject: Principles of Accounts
questions.text: An error of omission occurs when a transaction is
options: recorded with the correct amount but reversed between debit and credit
recorded twice by mistake, once in each of two different accounts
recorded in the wrong class of account, though the trial balance still balances
completely omitted from the books, with no entry made on either the debit or credit side
questions.explanation: An error of omission means a transaction is left out entirely, with neither a debit nor credit entry made, so the trial balance still balances despite the missing transaction.

questions.subject: Principles of Accounts
questions.text: An error of commission occurs when a transaction is
options: recorded correctly but the trial balance still fails to balance
entered in the correct class of account but posted to the wrong account within that class
recorded using the wrong fundamental accounting principle
completely left out of the accounting records
questions.explanation: An error of commission happens when the correct type of account is used, but the entry is posted to the wrong specific account, e.g., crediting the wrong individual customer's account.

questions.subject: Principles of Accounts
questions.text: An error of principle occurs when a transaction is
options: recorded twice in the same account
recorded but the two entries are simply swapped between debit and credit
recorded in a fundamentally wrong class of account, violating basic accounting principles
recorded in the correct account but with a transposed figure
questions.explanation: An error of principle involves misclassifying a transaction fundamentally, such as recording the purchase of an asset as an expense, violating the correct accounting treatment.

questions.subject: Principles of Accounts
questions.text: An error of original entry occurs when
options: an entry is posted to a completely wrong class of account
the same error is repeated across multiple different accounts
a transaction is completely left out of the books
the wrong amount is entered in the books of prime entry, though the double entry itself is otherwise correct
questions.explanation: In an error of original entry, an incorrect figure (perhaps due to misreading a source document) is used consistently for both the debit and credit sides, so the trial balance still balances despite the mistake.

questions.subject: Principles of Accounts
questions.text: A complete reversal of entries error occurs when
options: a transaction is entered twice in the same account
the debit and credit entries for a transaction are correctly valued but recorded on the wrong sides of the two accounts
a transaction is entirely omitted from the books
the wrong class of account entirely is used for a transaction
questions.explanation: In a complete reversal, the correct accounts and amount are used, but the debit and credit sides are swapped, meaning the trial balance still balances despite the transaction being effectively backwards.

questions.subject: Principles of Accounts
questions.text: A suspense account is opened mainly to
options: record all cash transactions of the business
permanently record errors that will never be corrected
replace the need for a trial balance
temporarily hold the difference when a trial balance fails to balance, until the error(s) causing it are found
questions.explanation: A suspense account is a temporary holding account used to balance the trial balance immediately, pending investigation and correction of the underlying one-sided error(s).

questions.subject: Principles of Accounts
questions.text: Which of the following errors would NOT affect the balancing of a trial balance?
options: Posting a debit entry without its corresponding credit entry
Recording only one side of a transaction in the ledger
Entering a debit twice without a corresponding credit
An error of complete omission
questions.explanation: Errors of omission, commission, principle, original entry, and complete reversal all affect both sides equally or not at all, so the trial balance still balances; only one-sided errors cause an imbalance.

questions.subject: Principles of Accounts
questions.text: If sales of N5,000 were recorded correctly in the Sales account but posted to the debtor's account as N500, this is an example of
options: an error of complete omission
an error of principle
an error of original entry
a compensating error
questions.explanation: Although this specific scenario involves inconsistent postings, the type where an incorrect original figure is carried consistently through the books is generally classified as an error of original entry.

questions.subject: Principles of Accounts
questions.text: Compensating errors occur when
options: a single error is corrected immediately upon discovery
two or more separate errors of equal and opposite amounts cancel each other out, so the trial balance still balances
all books of prime entry contain identical errors
an error affects only one side of the trial balance
questions.explanation: Compensating errors are unrelated mistakes that happen to be of equal and opposite value, masking each other's effect and allowing the trial balance to balance despite both errors being present.

questions.subject: Principles of Accounts
questions.text: Errors that are corrected via journal entries typically require a corresponding entry in the
options: sales journal only
suspense account, if the original error caused the trial balance to be out of balance
cash book only
purchases journal exclusively
questions.explanation: When correcting a one-sided error that was previously balanced off using a suspense account, the correcting journal entry must also involve the suspense account to finally clear it to zero.

questions.subject: Principles of Accounts
questions.text: The Trading Account of a sole trader is prepared mainly to calculate the
options: total value of fixed assets owned
net profit or net loss for the period
total amount owed to creditors
gross profit or gross loss for the period
questions.explanation: The Trading Account calculates gross profit (or loss) by comparing sales revenue against the cost of goods sold, before other operating expenses are considered.

questions.subject: Principles of Accounts
questions.text: Gross profit is calculated as
options: Sales minus Net Profit
Cost of Goods Sold minus Sales
Sales minus Cost of Goods Sold
Net Profit plus Expenses
questions.explanation: Gross Profit = Net Sales - Cost of Goods Sold, representing the profit made purely from trading activity before deducting other operating expenses.

questions.subject: Principles of Accounts
questions.text: Cost of goods sold is calculated as
options: Opening stock minus purchases plus closing stock
Sales minus gross profit
Opening stock plus purchases minus closing stock
Closing stock plus purchases minus opening stock
questions.explanation: Cost of Goods Sold = Opening Stock + Net Purchases - Closing Stock, representing the actual cost of the goods that were sold during the period.

questions.subject: Principles of Accounts
questions.text: A business has opening stock of N20,000, purchases of N80,000, and closing stock of N15,000. What is the cost of goods sold?
questions.explanation: Cost of Goods Sold = Opening Stock + Purchases - Closing Stock = 20,000 + 80,000 - 15,000 = N85,000.

questions.subject: Principles of Accounts
questions.text: The Profit and Loss Account of a sole trader is prepared to calculate the
options: total value of the business's assets
net profit or net loss after deducting operating expenses from gross profit
gross profit before any expenses are deducted
total capital contributed by the owner
questions.explanation: The Profit and Loss Account takes gross profit and deducts all other operating expenses (rent, salaries, utilities, etc.) to arrive at the final net profit or loss for the period.

questions.subject: Principles of Accounts
questions.text: A business has a gross profit of N50,000 and total operating expenses of N30,000. What is its net profit?
questions.explanation: Net Profit = Gross Profit - Operating Expenses = 50,000 - 30,000 = N20,000.

questions.subject: Principles of Accounts
questions.text: The Balance Sheet (Statement of Financial Position) of a business shows
options: only the cash transactions of the business
the profit or loss made over a period of time
only the sales made during the accounting period
the assets, liabilities, and capital of the business at a specific point in time
questions.explanation: Unlike the Trading and Profit and Loss Accounts (which cover a period), the Balance Sheet is a snapshot of the business's financial position (assets, liabilities, capital) at one specific date.

questions.subject: Principles of Accounts
questions.text: A prepaid expense at the end of an accounting period should be treated as
options: a current asset in the Balance Sheet and deducted from the expense in the Profit and Loss Account
a current liability in the Balance Sheet
an addition to the expense in the Profit and Loss Account
part of the closing stock figure
questions.explanation: A prepayment represents an amount paid in advance for a future period, so it is not yet a true expense of the current period, and represents a resource (asset) still owed to the business.

questions.subject: Principles of Accounts
questions.text: An accrued expense (expense owing) at the end of an accounting period should be treated as
options: part of the opening stock figure
a current asset in the Balance Sheet
a current liability in the Balance Sheet and added to the expense in the Profit and Loss Account
a deduction from the expense in the Profit and Loss Account
questions.explanation: An accrued expense has been incurred but not yet paid, so it represents money the business still owes (a liability) and must be included in the current period's expense figure.

questions.subject: Principles of Accounts
questions.text: Depreciation is best described as the
options: gradual reduction in the value of a fixed asset over its useful life
increase in the market value of a fixed asset over time
amount received when a fixed asset is sold
total cost of purchasing a new fixed asset
questions.explanation: Depreciation systematically allocates the cost of a fixed asset as an expense over the periods it is used, reflecting the wear, tear, or obsolescence of the asset over time.

questions.subject: Principles of Accounts
questions.text: Under the straight-line method of depreciation, the annual depreciation charge is calculated as
options: Cost of asset divided by the residual value
Residual value minus the cost of the asset
Cost of asset multiplied by the useful life
(Cost of asset - Residual value) divided by the estimated useful life
questions.explanation: The straight-line method spreads the depreciable amount (cost minus residual/scrap value) evenly across the asset's estimated useful life, giving a constant annual charge.

questions.subject: Principles of Accounts
questions.text: A machine costing N110,000 with an estimated residual value of N10,000 and a useful life of 5 years will have an annual straight-line depreciation charge of
questions.explanation: Annual depreciation = (Cost - Residual value)/Useful life = (110,000 - 10,000)/5 = 100,000/5 = N20,000.

questions.subject: Principles of Accounts
questions.text: A bad debt is an amount owed by a debtor that is
options: treated as an increase in the business's capital
considered irrecoverable and is written off as an expense
certain to be fully recovered in the future
always converted into a fixed asset
questions.explanation: When a debt is deemed unlikely ever to be collected, it is written off as a bad debt expense in the Profit and Loss Account, and removed from the debtors figure.

questions.subject: Principles of Accounts
questions.text: A provision for doubtful debts is created to
options: eliminate the need to ever write off a bad debt
increase the reported net profit artificially
record debts that have already been confirmed as completely uncollectible
anticipate potential future losses from debts that may not be collected, applying the prudence concept
questions.explanation: A provision for doubtful debts is an estimated allowance for debts that might not be recovered, applying the prudence concept by anticipating potential losses before they are certain.

questions.subject: Principles of Accounts
questions.text: A bank reconciliation statement is prepared mainly to
options: replace the need to maintain a cash book
record all credit sales made during a period
calculate the net profit of a business
explain and reconcile the difference between the balance shown in the cash book and the bank statement
questions.explanation: A bank reconciliation statement identifies and explains discrepancies between a business's own cash book balance and the balance shown on the bank's statement, ensuring both records are accurate.

questions.subject: Principles of Accounts
questions.text: Unpresented cheques, a common cause of discrepancy in bank reconciliation, refer to cheques that have been
options: cancelled and returned by the bank
already cleared by the bank but not yet recorded in the cash book
received and recorded in the cash book but not yet paid into the bank
issued and recorded in the cash book but have not yet been presented to the bank for payment
questions.explanation: Unpresented cheques have been written and deducted in the business's cash book, but the recipient has not yet cashed them, so they have not yet appeared on the bank statement.

questions.subject: Principles of Accounts
questions.text: Uncredited (unrealised) lodgements refer to deposits that have been
options: already cleared and reflected on both records
recorded on the bank statement but not yet in the cash book
returned by the bank due to insufficient funds
recorded in the cash book and paid into the bank but not yet reflected on the bank statement
questions.explanation: Uncredited lodgements are deposits the business has already recorded and banked, but which the bank has not yet processed and shown on its statement, often due to processing delays.

questions.subject: Principles of Accounts
questions.text: Bank charges deducted directly by the bank, which the business only discovers on receiving its bank statement, require which entry in the business's cash book?
options: An entry in the sales journal only
A credit entry to reduce the cash book balance to match the bank's records
A debit entry to increase the cash book balance
No entry is needed in the cash book at all
questions.explanation: Since bank charges reduce the business's actual bank balance, an adjusting credit entry must be made in the cash book to record this expense and bring the balance up to date.

questions.subject: Principles of Accounts
questions.text: A dishonoured cheque, one that a bank refuses to pay due to insufficient funds in the payer's account, must be
options: recorded only in the bank statement, never in the cash book
ignored completely since it was recorded correctly the first time
added back into the cash book as it no longer represents cash received
treated automatically as a bad debt with no further action needed
questions.explanation: When a cheque received is dishonoured, the amount previously treated as cash received must be reversed (added back) in the cash book, since the expected payment was not actually received.

questions.subject: Principles of Accounts
questions.text: Standing order payments made directly by the bank on behalf of the business, but not yet recorded in the cash book, require
options: a debit entry in the cash book to increase the balance
no adjustment, since standing orders are irrelevant to reconciliation
an adjustment only in the bank statement, not the cash book
a credit entry in the cash book to record the payment
questions.explanation: Since a standing order payment reduces the bank balance without the business separately recording it, a credit entry must be added to the cash book to reflect this outgoing payment.

questions.subject: Principles of Accounts
questions.text: Which of the following is a common cause of discrepancy between the cash book and bank statement balances?
options: Both records always being prepared identically at the same time
Timing differences, such as unpresented cheques and uncredited lodgements
The complete absence of any banking activity
Simultaneous recording of every transaction by both parties
questions.explanation: Most discrepancies arise from timing differences: transactions recorded by the business that have not yet been processed by the bank, or vice versa.

questions.subject: Principles of Accounts
questions.text: After preparing a bank reconciliation statement, the adjusted cash book balance should
options: equal the balance shown as reconciled on the bank statement
always be higher than the bank statement balance
always be lower than the bank statement balance
have no relationship at all to the bank statement balance
questions.explanation: The purpose of the reconciliation process is to adjust the cash book so that its final, corrected balance matches the balance confirmed on the bank statement after accounting for timing differences.

questions.subject: Principles of Accounts
questions.text: A Receipts and Payments Account, prepared by non-profit organisations, is essentially a summary of
options: the organisation's net profit or loss for the year
all cash and bank receipts and payments during a period, similar to a simple cash book summary
the organisation's total assets and liabilities
only the membership subscriptions received
questions.explanation: The Receipts and Payments Account simply summarises actual cash movements in and out of the organisation, similar to a cash book, without adjusting for accruals or prepayments.

questions.subject: Principles of Accounts
questions.text: An Income and Expenditure Account, prepared by non-profit organisations, is most similar in purpose to a
options: Profit and Loss Account of a trading business
Balance Sheet of a trading business
cash book of a trading business
Trading Account of a trading business
questions.explanation: The Income and Expenditure Account applies accrual accounting to determine a surplus or deficit for the period, serving the same function for a non-profit as a Profit and Loss Account does for a trading business.

questions.subject: Principles of Accounts
questions.text: A surplus in the Income and Expenditure Account of a non-profit organisation is equivalent to
options: capital contributed by members
net profit in a trading business's Profit and Loss Account
net loss in a trading business
gross profit in a trading business
questions.explanation: When an organisation's income exceeds its expenditure, the resulting positive balance is called a surplus, directly analogous to net profit in a commercial enterprise.

questions.subject: Principles of Accounts
questions.text: A deficit in the Income and Expenditure Account of a non-profit organisation is equivalent to
options: net loss in a trading business's Profit and Loss Account
net profit in a trading business
closing stock of a trading business
gross profit in a trading business
questions.explanation: A deficit occurs when an organisation's expenditure exceeds its income for the period, mirroring the concept of a net loss in a for-profit business.

questions.subject: Principles of Accounts
questions.text: Subscriptions received in advance from members should be treated in the accounts as a
options: current liability, since the organisation still owes the corresponding service for the future period
form of accumulated fund
current asset owned by the organisation
reduction in the organisation's expenditure
questions.explanation: Advance subscriptions relate to a future period, so they represent an obligation the organisation has not yet fully earned, making them a current liability until that period arrives.

questions.subject: Principles of Accounts
questions.text: Subscriptions owing (in arrears) from members at the end of the year should be treated as a
options: current asset in the Balance Sheet
current liability in the Balance Sheet
form of income received in advance
reduction in the accumulated fund
questions.explanation: Unpaid subscriptions still owed to the organisation represent a resource it is entitled to receive, making them a current asset (similar to a debtor) in the Balance Sheet.

questions.subject: Principles of Accounts
questions.text: The Accumulated Fund of a non-profit organisation is most similar in concept to the
options: creditors of a sole trader business
capital of a sole trader business
drawings of a sole trader business
cost of goods sold in a trading business
questions.explanation: The Accumulated Fund represents the net worth of a non-profit organisation built up over time from surpluses, membership fees, and donations, functioning much like capital does for a sole trader.

questions.subject: Principles of Accounts
questions.text: Life membership fees received by a club are generally treated as
options: a current liability that must be repaid to the member
an immediate, one-off expense for the year received
always excluded from the accounts entirely
income spread over a number of years, or added directly to the Accumulated Fund
questions.explanation: Since life membership provides benefits over many years, its fee is often treated as a capital receipt added to the Accumulated Fund, or spread as income over an estimated membership duration.

questions.subject: Principles of Accounts
questions.text: A partnership deed is a document that primarily sets out the
options: annual financial statements of the partnership
terms and conditions agreed upon by the partners governing the operation of the partnership
tax obligations of the partnership to the government
list of the partnership's customers
questions.explanation: The partnership deed (agreement) documents key terms such as profit-sharing ratios, capital contributions, interest on capital/drawings, and partners' salaries, guiding how the partnership is run.

questions.subject: Principles of Accounts
questions.text: In the absence of a partnership agreement, the Partnership Act generally states that profits and losses should be shared
options: in proportion to each partner's capital contribution
entirely by the partner with the most experience
according to the number of hours each partner works
equally among all partners
questions.explanation: Without a specific agreement stating otherwise, the default legal position under partnership law is that profits and losses are shared equally regardless of capital contributed.

questions.subject: Principles of Accounts
questions.text: A partner's Capital Account typically records
options: only the partner's salary entitlement
the partner's day-to-day drawings and share of profit
the total sales made by the partnership
the fixed amount of capital originally contributed by the partner to the business
questions.explanation: Under the fixed capital method, a partner's Capital Account remains relatively stable, recording only the original (and any additional) capital invested, while other movements go through the Current Account.

questions.subject: Principles of Accounts
questions.text: A partner's Current Account typically records
options: the total value of the partnership's fixed assets
the partnership's total liabilities
the partner's share of profit, interest on capital, salary, and drawings during the period
only the original capital invested by the partner
questions.explanation: The Current Account tracks the ongoing, fluctuating items relating to a partner (profit share, interest, salary, drawings), keeping the more stable Capital Account undisturbed.

questions.subject: Principles of Accounts
questions.text: The Profit and Loss Appropriation Account of a partnership is prepared to show how the
options: net profit of the partnership is distributed among the partners
gross profit of the partnership is calculated
partnership's fixed assets are valued
partnership's total liabilities are settled
questions.explanation: This account takes the net profit (carried over from the Profit and Loss Account) and allocates it among partners according to salaries, interest on capital, and the agreed profit-sharing ratio.

questions.subject: Principles of Accounts
questions.text: Interest on capital, when allowed to partners, is treated as
options: a business expense deducted before arriving at net profit
a form of partnership liability to outside creditors
a reduction in the partner's capital contribution
an appropriation of profit, not a business expense
questions.explanation: Interest on capital is a way of distributing (appropriating) the already-calculated net profit among partners to reward their capital investment, rather than being treated as an expense of the business itself.

questions.subject: Principles of Accounts
questions.text: Interest on drawings, when charged to partners, is
options: added back to the profit available for appropriation among the partners
treated as a business expense in the Profit and Loss Account
ignored entirely in partnership accounts
deducted from the total net profit before appropriation
questions.explanation: Interest charged on partners' drawings compensates the partnership for money withdrawn early, and is added back into the pool of profit available for distribution among the partners.

questions.subject: Principles of Accounts
questions.text: When a new partner is admitted into an existing partnership, goodwill is typically
options: automatically transferred entirely to the new partner
valued and adjusted to compensate the existing partners for the value built up in the business before the new partner joined
always written off completely with no adjustment made
irrelevant to the accounting treatment of the admission
questions.explanation: Goodwill represents the value of an established partnership's reputation and customer base; existing partners are compensated for sharing this built-up value with an incoming partner.

questions.subject: Principles of Accounts
questions.text: When a partner retires from a partnership, the amount due to them typically includes their
options: personal, non-business related assets
share of the partnership's total liabilities alone
salary for the following year only
capital balance, current account balance, and share of any goodwill or revaluation profit
questions.explanation: A retiring partner is generally entitled to their accumulated capital, current account balance, and an appropriate share of goodwill and any profit or loss arising from revaluing partnership assets.

questions.subject: Principles of Accounts
questions.text: The profit-sharing ratio of a partnership refers to the
options: ratio of a partner's capital to the total liabilities
agreed proportion in which partners share the net profit or loss of the business
ratio used to calculate depreciation on partnership assets
proportion of sales made by each individual partner
questions.explanation: The profit-sharing ratio specifies exactly how the partnership's net profit (or loss) is divided among the partners, as agreed in the partnership deed.

questions.subject: Principles of Accounts
questions.text: A share represents
options: a document confirming a customer's purchase
a type of company expense
a loan given to the company that must be repaid with interest
a unit of ownership in a company
questions.explanation: Shares represent fractional ownership stakes in a company, entitling holders to a portion of profits (dividends) and, often, voting rights, unlike debentures, which represent debt.

questions.subject: Principles of Accounts
questions.text: An ordinary share typically entitles the holder to
options: guaranteed repayment of their investment with interest
priority over all other shareholders in every circumstance
a variable dividend depending on company profits, and voting rights at general meetings
a fixed rate of dividend regardless of company profits
questions.explanation: Ordinary shareholders typically receive dividends that vary based on company performance and profitability, and usually have voting rights in company matters.

questions.subject: Principles of Accounts
questions.text: A preference share typically entitles the holder to
options: automatic conversion into a company director role
an unlimited, variable share of company profits
voting rights that exceed those of ordinary shareholders
a fixed rate of dividend, paid before ordinary shareholders receive theirs
questions.explanation: Preference shareholders generally receive a fixed dividend rate and are paid before ordinary shareholders, though they typically have limited or no voting rights in return for this priority.

questions.subject: Principles of Accounts
questions.text: A debenture represents
options: a unit of ownership in the company
a loan to the company, on which fixed interest must be paid regardless of profit
a form of company profit distributed to shareholders
a government tax imposed on the company
questions.explanation: Unlike shares, debentures represent borrowed money (debt), and the company is obligated to pay fixed interest on them whether or not it makes a profit.

questions.subject: Principles of Accounts
questions.text: A key difference between shares and debentures is that debenture holders are
options: creditors of the company, while shareholders are owners of the company
always paid dividends before any interest is paid to anyone
entitled to vote at company meetings, unlike ordinary shareholders
owners of the company, while shareholders are creditors
questions.explanation: Debenture holders have lent money to the company and are therefore its creditors with a claim to interest, whereas shareholders are part-owners entitled to a share of profits (dividends).

questions.subject: Principles of Accounts
questions.text: Dividends paid to shareholders are best described as a
options: distribution of a company's profit to its owners
fixed interest payment owed regardless of profitability
compulsory expense deducted before calculating net profit
form of tax paid to the government
questions.explanation: Dividends represent the portion of a company's after-tax profit that is distributed to shareholders as a reward for their investment, rather than being treated as a business expense.

questions.subject: Principles of Accounts
questions.text: A Manufacturing Account is prepared mainly by businesses that
options: purchase finished goods solely for resale
operate exclusively as non-profit organisations
produce their own goods, to calculate the cost of production for the period
provide services only, without producing physical goods
questions.explanation: Manufacturing businesses prepare this account to determine the total cost of manufacturing (producing) goods during a period, before those goods are then sold and accounted for in the Trading Account.

questions.subject: Principles of Accounts
questions.text: Direct materials, in the context of a Manufacturing Account, refer to
options: raw materials that can be directly and easily traced to the finished product
administrative expenses of the factory office
the salary of the factory manager
the cost of factory rent and utilities
questions.explanation: Direct materials are raw materials that become an identifiable, traceable part of the finished product, as distinct from general factory overheads or indirect materials.

questions.subject: Principles of Accounts
questions.text: Prime cost in a Manufacturing Account is calculated as
options: Total factory cost minus direct labour
Direct materials minus factory overheads
Direct materials plus direct labour plus direct expenses
Direct labour plus indirect factory overheads
questions.explanation: Prime cost represents the total of all costs directly attributable to production: direct materials, direct labour, and any other direct expenses specifically tied to manufacturing.

questions.subject: Principles of Accounts
questions.text: Factory overheads (indirect manufacturing costs) include expenses such as
options: direct materials used in production
sales commissions paid to sales staff
factory rent, factory power, and depreciation of factory machinery
wages paid directly to production line workers
questions.explanation: Factory overheads consist of indirect costs necessary for production but not directly traceable to specific units, such as factory rent, utilities, and machinery depreciation.

questions.subject: Principles of Accounts
questions.text: The total production cost in a Manufacturing Account is calculated as
options: Prime cost minus factory overheads
Direct materials only
Prime cost plus factory overheads
Factory overheads minus direct labour
questions.explanation: Total (factory) cost of production combines the prime cost (direct costs) with the indirect factory overheads incurred during the manufacturing process.

questions.subject: Principles of Accounts
questions.text: The cost of raw materials consumed during a period is calculated as
options: Opening stock of raw materials minus purchases of raw materials
Closing stock of raw materials plus purchases minus opening stock
Purchases of raw materials alone, ignoring stock changes
Opening stock of raw materials plus purchases of raw materials minus closing stock of raw materials
questions.explanation: Similar to the cost of goods sold calculation, raw materials consumed = opening stock + purchases - closing stock of raw materials, reflecting materials actually used in production.

questions.subject: Principles of Accounts
questions.text: Incomplete records refer to a situation where a business
options: has ceased trading entirely
does not maintain a full, formal double-entry bookkeeping system
operates exclusively as a large public limited company
keeps perfectly complete and accurate double-entry accounts
questions.explanation: Many small businesses, especially sole traders, keep only partial or informal records rather than a complete double-entry system, requiring special techniques to determine their financial position.

questions.subject: Principles of Accounts
questions.text: The statement of affairs method is used to calculate a business's profit by comparing its
options: fixed assets at cost versus their market value
cash receipts and cash payments only
capital at the start and end of the accounting period, adjusted for drawings and additional capital introduced
total sales and total purchases for the period
questions.explanation: Since full accounts are unavailable, profit is deduced indirectly by comparing opening and closing capital (net assets), adjusting for any drawings taken out and additional capital paid in during the period.

questions.subject: Principles of Accounts
questions.text: The formula for calculating profit under the statement of affairs (net worth) method is
options: Closing capital minus opening capital only, with no other adjustments
Opening capital plus drawings minus closing capital
Closing capital minus drawings plus additional capital introduced minus opening capital
Closing capital plus drawings minus additional capital introduced minus opening capital
questions.explanation: Profit = (Closing Capital + Drawings) - (Opening Capital + Additional Capital Introduced), since drawings reduce capital that must be added back, and new capital introduced must be excluded from the profit figure.

questions.subject: Principles of Accounts
questions.text: A business had an opening capital of N100,000 and a closing capital of N160,000. During the year, the owner made drawings of N20,000 and introduced no additional capital. What was the profit for the year?
questions.explanation: Profit = (Closing Capital + Drawings) - Opening Capital = (160,000 + 20,000) - 100,000 = 180,000 - 100,000 = N80,000.

questions.subject: Principles of Accounts
questions.text: A machine costing N250,000 has an estimated residual value of N30,000 and a useful life of 8 years. Using the straight-line method, what is the annual depreciation charge?
questions.explanation: Annual depreciation = (Cost - Residual value)/Useful life = (250,000 - 30,000)/8 = 220,000/8 = N27,500.

questions.subject: Principles of Accounts
questions.text: An asset costing N100,000 is depreciated at 20% per annum using the reducing balance method. What is the depreciation charge for the second year?
questions.explanation: Year 1 depreciation = 20% x 100,000 = 20,000, leaving a net book value of 80,000. Year 2 depreciation = 20% x 80,000 = N16,000.

questions.subject: Principles of Accounts
questions.text: A machine costing N200,000 is depreciated at 10% per annum on the reducing balance basis. What is its net book value at the end of the second year?

questions.subject: Principles of Accounts
questions.text: A machine costing N150,000 with no residual value is depreciated over 10 years using the straight-line method. What is its net book value after 3 years?
questions.explanation: Annual depreciation = 150,000/10 = 15,000. After 3 years, accumulated depreciation = 45,000, so net book value = 150,000 - 45,000 = N105,000.

questions.subject: Principles of Accounts
questions.text: Compared with the straight-line method, the reducing balance method of depreciation
options: charges a higher depreciation amount in the earlier years of the asset's life, while the straight-line method charges an equal amount every year
always charges a lower depreciation amount throughout the asset's life
produces exactly the same annual charge as the straight-line method
can never be applied to motor vehicles or machinery
questions.explanation: The reducing balance method applies a fixed percentage to a declining net book value, so it charges more depreciation early in an asset's life and progressively less, unlike the straight-line method's constant annual charge.

questions.subject: Principles of Accounts
questions.text: A provision for depreciation account had an opening balance of N60,000. During the year, N15,000 depreciation was charged, and an asset with accumulated depreciation of N10,000 was disposed of. What is the closing balance of the provision for depreciation account?
questions.explanation: Closing balance = Opening balance + Depreciation charged for the year - Accumulated depreciation removed on disposal = 60,000 + 15,000 - 10,000 = N65,000.

questions.subject: Principles of Accounts
questions.text: An asset costing N80,000 is depreciated using the straight-line method at a rate of 25% of cost per annum. What is its net book value after 2 years?
questions.explanation: Annual depreciation = 25% x 80,000 = 20,000. After 2 years, accumulated depreciation = 40,000, so net book value = 80,000 - 40,000 = N40,000.

questions.subject: Principles of Accounts
questions.text: Using the reducing balance method at a rate of 20% per annum, an asset's first-year depreciation charge was N18,000. What was the original cost of the asset?
questions.explanation: In the first year, the reducing balance rate is applied to the full cost. Cost = Depreciation charge / Rate = 18,000/0.20 = N90,000.

questions.subject: Principles of Accounts
questions.text: In the earlier years of an asset's life, which depreciation method typically results in a lower reported net profit for a business, all else being equal?
options: The reducing balance method, because it charges a higher depreciation amount in the earlier years of the asset's life
The straight-line method, because it charges a higher depreciation amount every year
Both methods always produce identical profit figures in every year
Neither method affects the reported net profit of a business
questions.explanation: Because the reducing balance method front-loads larger depreciation charges into the early years of an asset's life, it reduces reported net profit more than the straight-line method during that period.

questions.subject: Principles of Accounts
questions.text: A machine costing N96,000 has a residual value of N6,000 and a useful life of 6 years, depreciated by the straight-line method. What is its net book value after 4 years?
questions.explanation: Annual depreciation = (96,000 - 6,000)/6 = 15,000. After 4 years, accumulated depreciation = 60,000, so net book value = 96,000 - 60,000 = N36,000.

questions.subject: Principles of Accounts
questions.text: An asset that cost N50,000 has accumulated depreciation of N20,000 and is sold for N35,000. What is the profit or loss on disposal?
options: Loss of N30,000
Profit of N15,000
Profit of N5,000
Loss of N35,000
questions.explanation: Net book value = 50,000 - 20,000 = 30,000. Since the asset was sold for 35,000, profit on disposal = 35,000 - 30,000 = N5,000.

questions.subject: Principles of Accounts
questions.text: An asset that cost N40,000 has accumulated depreciation of N25,000 and is sold for N9,000. What is the profit or loss on disposal?
options: Profit of N15,000
Loss of N9,000
Profit of N25,000
Loss of N6,000
questions.explanation: Net book value = 40,000 - 25,000 = 15,000. Since the asset was sold for only 9,000, loss on disposal = 15,000 - 9,000 = N6,000.

questions.subject: Principles of Accounts
questions.text: A trial balance shows total debits of N500,000 and total credits of N480,000. If a suspense account is opened to make the trial balance balance, it will show
options: a credit balance of N20,000
a debit balance of N20,000
a debit balance of N40,000
a credit balance of N10,000
questions.explanation: Since total debits (500,000) exceed total credits (480,000) by 20,000, a suspense account with a credit balance of N20,000 is opened to bring the credit column up to 500,000.

questions.subject: Principles of Accounts
questions.text: Which pair of errors, occurring simultaneously, would be classified as compensating errors that still allow the trial balance to balance?
options: A cheque payment posted twice to the same creditor's account only
The Purchases account overcast by N500 and the Sales account overcast by N500
A sales invoice completely omitted from all the books
A credit purchase posted to the debit of the Purchases account but omitted from the supplier's account
questions.explanation: Overcasting the Purchases account (an extra debit of 500) and overcasting the Sales account (an extra credit of 500) are unrelated errors of equal and opposite value that cancel out, so the trial balance still balances.

questions.subject: Principles of Accounts
questions.text: A trial balance failed to balance because total debits were N3,000 less than total credits, so a suspense account was opened with a debit balance of N3,000. It was later discovered that a sales return of N3,000 had been completely omitted from the Sales Returns account. What correcting journal entry clears the suspense account?
options: Debit Suspense account N3,000; Credit Sales Returns account N3,000
Debit Sales account N3,000; Credit Suspense account N3,000
Debit Sales Returns account N3,000; Credit Suspense account N3,000
Debit Suspense account N3,000; Credit Sales account N3,000
questions.explanation: Sales Returns should have been debited N3,000 but was omitted, leaving the debit side short. Debiting Sales Returns and crediting Suspense N3,000 corrects the omission and clears the suspense account to zero.

questions.subject: Principles of Accounts
questions.text: A credit purchase invoice of N5,400 was entered in the Purchases Day Book as N4,500 due to a transposition of digits, and this figure was posted consistently to both the Purchases account and the supplier's account. As a result,
options: the trial balance will fail to balance by N900
the trial balance will still balance, but only the Purchases account will be affected
the trial balance will fail to balance by N1,800
the trial balance will still balance, but both the Purchases account and the supplier's account will be understated by N900
questions.explanation: Since the same wrong figure (4,500 instead of 5,400) was used for both the debit and credit sides, the trial balance still balances, but both the Purchases account and the supplier's account are understated by 5,400 - 4,500 = N900.

questions.subject: Principles of Accounts
questions.text: A bank statement shows a balance of N52,000. Cheques of N10,000 issued by the business have not yet been presented for payment, and deposits of N3,000 paid in have not yet been credited by the bank. What is the balance shown in the cash book?
questions.explanation: Cash book balance = Bank statement balance - Unpresented cheques + Uncredited lodgements = 52,000 - 10,000 + 3,000 = N45,000.

questions.subject: Principles of Accounts
questions.text: A cash book shows a debit balance of N38,000 before reconciliation. On comparing it with the bank statement, it is found that bank charges of N1,500 and a standing order payment of N2,500 have not been recorded in the cash book, and that a customer's cheque for N4,000 previously credited was dishonoured. What is the adjusted (corrected) cash book balance?
questions.explanation: Adjusted balance = 38,000 - 1,500 (bank charges) - 2,500 (standing order) - 4,000 (dishonoured cheque) = N30,000.

questions.subject: Principles of Accounts
questions.text: The cash book balance of a business is N60,000. Cheques drawn amounting to N15,000 have not yet been presented for payment, while lodgements of N5,000 have not yet been credited by the bank. What balance would appear on the bank statement?
questions.explanation: Bank statement balance = Cash book balance + Unpresented cheques - Uncredited lodgements = 60,000 + 15,000 - 5,000 = N70,000.

questions.subject: Principles of Accounts
questions.text: A cash book showed a debtor's cheque of N12,000 recorded as cash received, giving a cash book balance of N55,000. The cheque was later dishonoured by the bank. What should the corrected cash book balance be?
questions.explanation: A dishonoured cheque means the expected receipt did not materialise, so the amount must be deducted again: 55,000 - 12,000 = N43,000.

questions.subject: Principles of Accounts
questions.text: A cheque payment of N7,500 was entered in the cash book as N5,700 due to transposition of digits. If the cash book balance before correction was N40,000, what is the corrected balance?
questions.explanation: The payment was understated by 7,500 - 5,700 = 1,800, meaning too little was deducted, so the cash book balance is overstated by that amount: 40,000 - 1,800 = N38,200.

questions.subject: Principles of Accounts
questions.text: A bank statement shows a direct credit transfer of N5,000 received from a customer, which has not yet been entered in the business's cash book. If the cash book balance before this adjustment was N32,000, what is the adjusted cash book balance?
questions.explanation: A direct credit received by the bank but not yet recorded by the business increases the cash book balance: 32,000 + 5,000 = N37,000.

questions.subject: Principles of Accounts
questions.text: A business's cash book shows a balance of N90,000, while the bank statement shows a balance of N100,000. Given that uncredited lodgements amount to N15,000, what is the value of unpresented cheques?
questions.explanation: Cash book balance = Bank statement balance - Unpresented cheques + Uncredited lodgements, so 90,000 = 100,000 - x + 15,000, giving x = 100,000 + 15,000 - 90,000 = N25,000.

questions.subject: Principles of Accounts
questions.text: A business's cash book shows a balance of N70,000, while the bank statement shows a balance of N65,000. Given that unpresented cheques amount to N12,000, what is the value of uncredited lodgements?
questions.explanation: Cash book balance = Bank statement balance - Unpresented cheques + Uncredited lodgements, so 70,000 = 65,000 - 12,000 + x, giving x = 70,000 - 65,000 + 12,000 = N17,000.

questions.subject: Principles of Accounts
questions.text: Before preparing a bank reconciliation statement, a business first updates (adjusts) its cash book. This step is necessary in order to
options: correct entries relating to bank charges, standing orders, dishonoured cheques, and direct bank credits that the business has not yet recorded, while timing differences are shown in the reconciliation statement itself
eliminate the need for a bank reconciliation statement entirely
record every transaction appearing on the bank statement a second time
convert the cash book into a trial balance
questions.explanation: Items the bank has processed but the business has not yet recorded (bank charges, standing orders, dishonoured cheques, direct credits) must first be entered in the cash book, while timing differences (unpresented cheques, uncredited lodgements) are dealt with separately in the reconciliation statement.

questions.subject: Principles of Accounts
questions.text: A business has sales of N400,000 and cost of goods sold of N280,000. What is its gross profit margin (as a percentage of sales)?

questions.subject: Principles of Accounts
questions.text: A business has sales of N500,000 and net profit of N75,000. What is its net profit margin?
questions.explanation: Net profit margin = Net profit/Sales x 100 = 75,000/500,000 x 100 = 15.0%.

questions.subject: Principles of Accounts
questions.text: Goods costing N80,000 are marked up by 25% on cost to determine the selling price. What is the resulting gross profit margin, expressed as a percentage of selling price?
questions.explanation: Profit = 25% x 80,000 = 20,000, so selling price = 100,000. Margin (on selling price) = 20,000/100,000 x 100 = 20.0%, which differs from the 25% mark-up (on cost).

questions.subject: Principles of Accounts
questions.text: A business has current assets of N150,000 and current liabilities of N75,000. What is its current ratio?
questions.explanation: Current ratio = Current assets : Current liabilities = 150,000:75,000 = 2:1.

questions.subject: Principles of Accounts
questions.text: A business has current assets of N150,000 (including stock of N60,000) and current liabilities of N75,000. What is its acid-test (quick) ratio?
questions.explanation: Quick assets = Current assets - Stock = 150,000 - 60,000 = 90,000. Acid-test ratio = 90,000/75,000 = 1.2:1.

questions.subject: Principles of Accounts
questions.text: A business has a cost of goods sold of N240,000 and an average stock of N40,000. What is its rate of stock turnover?
options: 4 times
8 times
6 times
10 times
questions.explanation: Rate of stock turnover = Cost of goods sold/Average stock = 240,000/40,000 = 6 times per year.

questions.subject: Principles of Accounts
questions.text: A business had an opening stock of N30,000 and a closing stock of N50,000. What is its average stock for the period?
questions.explanation: Average stock = (Opening stock + Closing stock)/2 = (30,000 + 50,000)/2 = N40,000.

questions.subject: Principles of Accounts
questions.text: A business reports sales of N300,000, opening stock of N20,000, purchases of N150,000, closing stock of N25,000, and operating expenses of N60,000. What is its net profit for the period?

questions.subject: Principles of Accounts
questions.text: A business paid N12,000 for insurance on 1 October, covering 12 months from that date. If the accounting year ends on 31 December, what amount should be treated as a prepayment (current asset) in the Balance Sheet?
questions.explanation: Monthly cost = 12,000/12 = 1,000. Only 3 months (October to December) relate to the current year, so the expense is 3,000 and the remaining 9 months (9,000) is a prepayment carried forward as a current asset.

questions.subject: Principles of Accounts
questions.text: A business paid rent of N40,000 during the year, but at the year end a further N5,000 was owing for rent relating to the period covered. What amount should appear as the rent expense in the Profit and Loss Account, and how should the N5,000 be treated in the Balance Sheet?
options: N40,000 as expense; N5,000 shown as a current asset
N35,000 as expense; N5,000 shown as a current liability
N45,000 as expense; N5,000 shown as a current liability
N45,000 as expense; N5,000 shown as a current asset
questions.explanation: The full amount incurred (accrual concept) must be charged: 40,000 + 5,000 = N45,000 expense, with the unpaid N5,000 shown as a current liability (accrued expense) owed at year end.

questions.subject: Principles of Accounts
questions.text: A business has debtors of N60,000 and an existing provision for doubtful debts of N2,000. It now wishes to maintain a provision equal to 5% of debtors. What is the increase in the provision to be charged to the Profit and Loss Account?
questions.explanation: Required provision = 5% x 60,000 = 3,000. Since the existing provision is 2,000, the increase to be charged as an additional expense is 3,000 - 2,000 = N1,000.

questions.subject: Principles of Accounts
questions.text: A business has debtors of N82,000 before adjustments. It is decided to write off further bad debts of N2,000 and then create a provision for doubtful debts of 5% of the remaining debtors. What is the amount of the new provision for doubtful debts?
questions.explanation: Debtors after writing off bad debts = 82,000 - 2,000 = 80,000. Provision = 5% x 80,000 = N4,000.

questions.subject: Principles of Accounts
questions.text: Fixtures and fittings costing N60,000 are to be depreciated at 10% per annum using the straight-line method when preparing the final accounts. How should this be treated?
options: N6,000 added to sales revenue in the Trading Account
N6,000 charged as an expense in the Profit and Loss Account, and deducted from the asset in the Balance Sheet
N60,000 charged in full as an expense immediately
N6,000 treated as a current liability in the Balance Sheet
questions.explanation: Depreciation = 10% x 60,000 = 6,000, which is charged as an expense in the Profit and Loss Account and deducted from the asset's cost (as accumulated depreciation) in the Balance Sheet.

questions.subject: Principles of Accounts
questions.text: A business has fixed assets of N220,000, current assets of N90,000, current liabilities of N40,000, and long-term liabilities of N50,000. What is the value of the owner's capital?

questions.subject: Principles of Accounts
questions.text: A business has current assets of N130,000 and current liabilities of N85,000. What is its working capital?
questions.explanation: Working capital = Current assets - Current liabilities = 130,000 - 85,000 = N45,000.

questions.subject: Principles of Accounts
questions.text: A business has a net profit of N60,000 and capital employed of N400,000. What is its return on capital employed (ROCE)?
questions.explanation: ROCE = Net profit/Capital employed x 100 = 60,000/400,000 x 100 = 15%.

questions.subject: Principles of Accounts
questions.text: A business's cost of sales is N180,000, and this represents 75% of its sales value (since gross profit margin is 25% of sales). What is the value of sales?
questions.explanation: Sales = Cost of sales/(1 - margin) = 180,000/0.75 = N240,000, giving gross profit of 240,000 - 180,000 = 60,000, which is indeed 25% of 240,000.

questions.subject: Principles of Accounts
questions.text: Goods costing N150,000 are marked up by 20% on cost. What is the resulting gross profit margin, expressed as a percentage of the selling price (to one decimal place)?
questions.explanation: Profit = 20% x 150,000 = 30,000, so selling price = 180,000. Margin = 30,000/180,000 x 100 = 16.7%, illustrating that a mark-up on cost always gives a smaller percentage margin on selling price.

questions.subject: Principles of Accounts
questions.text: A business has sales of N500,000 and a gross profit margin of 40%. What is its cost of goods sold?
questions.explanation: Gross profit = 40% x 500,000 = 200,000. Cost of goods sold = Sales - Gross profit = 500,000 - 200,000 = N300,000.

questions.subject: Principles of Accounts
questions.text: A trader bought goods for N100,000 and paid carriage inwards of N5,000. Opening stock was N10,000 and closing stock was N15,000. Sales for the period were N180,000, carriage outwards was N3,000, and other operating expenses were N20,000. What was the net profit for the period?
questions.explanation: Adjusted purchases = 100,000 + 5,000 = 105,000. Cost of goods sold = 10,000 + 105,000 - 15,000 = 100,000. Gross profit = 180,000 - 100,000 = 80,000. Net profit = 80,000 - 3,000 (carriage outwards) - 20,000 (other expenses) = N57,000.

questions.subject: Principles of Accounts
questions.text: A sole trader made purchases of N200,000 during the year, but withdrew goods costing N8,000 for personal use. How should this drawing of goods be treated in the final accounts?
options: Ignored completely since no cash changed hands
Deducted from purchases in the Trading Account (leaving N192,000), and added to the owner's drawings
Added to purchases in the Trading Account, and shown as an increase in debtors
Deducted from sales revenue for the period
questions.explanation: Goods taken by the owner are not a business expense or sale; they are deducted from purchases (200,000 - 8,000 = 192,000) to correctly state the cost of goods available for sale, and recorded as an increase in the owner's drawings.

questions.subject: Principles of Accounts
questions.text: A business has fixed assets of N250,000, current assets of N100,000, and current liabilities of N50,000. What is its capital employed?
questions.explanation: Capital employed = Fixed assets + Working capital = 250,000 + (100,000 - 50,000) = 250,000 + 50,000 = N300,000.

questions.subject: Principles of Accounts
questions.text: Over two years, a business's gross profit margin fell slightly, while its net profit margin fell much more sharply. What does this most likely indicate?
options: Cost of goods sold decreased significantly relative to sales
The business's sales figure was recorded incorrectly both years
The business's current ratio improved significantly
Operating expenses increased significantly relative to sales
questions.explanation: Since the gap between gross and net profit is operating expenses, a much sharper fall in net profit margin than gross profit margin points to operating expenses rising disproportionately relative to sales.

questions.subject: Principles of Accounts
questions.text: A business has an average stock of N60,000 and a cost of goods sold of N360,000 for the year. What is its average stock turnover period, in days (to the nearest day)?
options: 61 days
36 days
72 days
50 days
questions.explanation: Stock turnover = 360,000/60,000 = 6 times per year. Stock turnover period = 365/6 = approximately 61 days.

questions.subject: Principles of Accounts
questions.text: A business has debtors of N45,000 and credit sales of N300,000 for the year. What is its average debtors' collection period, in days (to the nearest day)?
options: 45 days
55 days
60 days
75 days
questions.explanation: Collection period = (Debtors/Credit sales) x 365 = (45,000/300,000) x 365 = 0.15 x 365 = approximately 55 days.

questions.subject: Principles of Accounts
questions.text: Partners A and B have capitals of N100,000 and N80,000 respectively, and interest on capital is allowed at 10% per annum. The net profit available for appropriation is N90,000, and after interest on capital, the remaining profit is shared equally. What total amount (interest plus profit share) is credited to Partner A?
questions.explanation: Interest on capital: A = 10% x 100,000 = 10,000; B = 10% x 80,000 = 8,000, totalling 18,000. Remaining profit = 90,000 - 18,000 = 72,000, split equally = 36,000 each. A's total = 10,000 + 36,000 = N46,000.

questions.subject: Principles of Accounts
questions.text: Partner C is entitled to an annual salary of N18,000 before the remaining profit is shared between C and D in the ratio 3:2. If the net profit available for appropriation is N60,000, what is C's total share (salary plus profit share)?
questions.explanation: Remaining profit after salary = 60,000 - 18,000 = 42,000. C's share of the remaining profit = 42,000 x 3/5 = 25,200. C's total = 18,000 + 25,200 = N43,200.

questions.subject: Principles of Accounts
questions.text: A partner made drawings of N10,000 during the year, and the partnership charges interest on drawings at 5% per annum. How should this interest on drawings be treated in the Profit and Loss Appropriation Account?
options: Added back to the profit available for appropriation among the partners
Deducted from the net profit before appropriation
Ignored, since drawings do not attract interest
Treated as an expense in the Trading Account
questions.explanation: Interest on drawings (5% x 10,000 = 500) is charged to the partner and added back into the pool of profit available for distribution among all partners, increasing the amount to be appropriated.

questions.subject: Principles of Accounts
questions.text: A partner's current account had an opening credit balance of N5,000. During the year, interest on capital of N2,000 and a profit share of N15,000 were credited, while drawings of N8,000 and interest on drawings of N300 were debited. What is the closing balance of the current account?

questions.subject: Principles of Accounts
questions.text: Partners X and Y share profits in the ratio 3:2. A new partner is admitted, and the goodwill of the business is valued at N60,000.
